author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: Larry Brewster, drinking alone in a bar, is approached by the poised, unhurried Allison Holmes, who calmly explains a solipsistic philosophy: each person inhabits their own private world in which they alone are wholly real, while everyone else exists only partially, arranged for their happiness.
page_summary:
Larry Brewster, drinking alone in a bar, is approached by the poised, unhurried Allison Holmes, who calmly explains a solipsistic philosophy: each person inhabits their own private world in which they alone are wholly real, while everyone else exists only partially, arranged for their happiness. Over a whirlwind courtship everything effortlessly bends to her wishes -- free drinks, an inherited mansion, a remade gambling club, Larry's favorite bar tastelessly 'improved' for her comfort -- while Larry grows increasingly uneasy at how thoroughly his own familiar world is being rearranged around her. When he finally tries to break away, Allison warns him that he cannot leave, since in her world he is not fully real to begin with. He answers, quietly and with total certainty, that she is the one leaving -- and a ball of light erases her from existence in front of him, revealing that Larry, not Allison, possesses the reality-shaping power, that this has been his world all along, and that she had only ever been partly real within it.

**Why it matters.** The story takes solipsism -- ordinarily a philosophical thought experiment -- and stages it as a literal contest of realities, in which two people can each sincerely believe themselves the sole fully-real center of a shared world, with only one of them actually correct. Its explicit invocations of Descartes and Plato mark the premise as a deliberate engagement with philosophical idealism rather than an incidental fantasy device, and the story's cruelty lies in how completely Allison's belief is validated by circumstance right up until the instant it is disproven -- she is not merely wrong, she is annihilated for having been wrong, with no warning that the contest was even underway. Larry's own reality-shaping power remains entirely latent and unconscious until the final page, raising the story's most unsettling implication: that a person may possess such power without ever suspecting it, only discovering it in the act of exercising it against someone else.

*Larry's flat, certain reply -- 'No... you're leaving' -- and the wordless ball of light that follows leave his own reaction to what he has just done entirely unexplored; the story ends at the moment of revelation rather than showing what Larry does with the power, or the solitude, he now understands to be his.*

structure.form: short story in three movements: Allison's solipsistic philosophy delivered as a seduction, the courtship's escalating and unsettling wish-fulfillment, and the reversal that exposes whose world it actually is
movements: In a bar, Allison Holmes explains to Larry Brewster a philosophy in which each person's private world alone is fully real, and everyone else in it exists only partially, arranged for that person's benefit.

Their courtship proceeds through a string of frictionless, wish-granting coincidences and unrequested improvements -- to a mansion, a club, Larry's favorite bar -- that leave Larry disturbed rather than delighted.

When Larry tries to leave her, Allison insists he cannot, since he is not fully real in what she believes is her world; Larry calmly tells her that she is the one leaving, and a ball of light erases her from existence, revealing the world was his all along.
structure.point_of_view: third person close to Larry throughout, so his mounting unease at a world being reshaped for someone else's comfort reads as ordinary romantic claustrophobia right up until the story's closing reversal recontextualizes every prior scene as evidence of his own latent power rather than hers.
structure.central_device: A solipsistic metaphysics stated openly and taken at face value by both characters, used as a courtship script that each partner assumes describes their own privileged reality -- until the story's final beat reveals that only one of them was ever actually right.

characters.name: Larry Brewster
characters.note: His discomfort with Allison's effortless remaking of his world is initially legible as ordinary anxiety about a controlling partner, but the ending reframes it as the friction of someone else's delusion pressing against a reality that was never actually hers to alter.

characters.name: Allison Holmes
characters.note: Her calm, unshakeable conviction that she alone is fully real and everyone else exists to serve her happiness is presented without irony for most of the story -- and is validated by every convenient coincidence that follows her, right up until the moment it is fatally disproven.

settings.name: Larry's favorite bar
settings.note: Its unrequested, tasteless remodeling 'for' Allison's comfort is the story's clearest early signal that reality itself is being bent around her presence, at the cost of Larry's own attachment to how things used to be.

settings.name: The inherited mansion
settings.note: Its sudden, convenient appearance in Allison's life -- like the remade gambling club -- reads as further proof of her reality-warping solipsism, though the ending recasts every such convenience as ultimately serving Larry's own hidden power instead.

motifs: A solipsistic philosophy -- one true self surrounded by partially real others existing for that self's benefit -- stated plainly and acted out literally rather than left as abstract metaphor
Reality reshaping itself frictionlessly around a character's desires, initially read as romantic good fortune before being exposed as evidence of unacknowledged power
A courtship in which each partner assumes the other is the fully real one, with catastrophic consequences once the assumption is corrected
Erasure from existence as the literal, final consequence of losing a contest neither party knew they were having

distinctive_terms.label: Creator
distinctive_terms.note: The story's high concentration of this term tracks its central metaphysical claim -- that a person's private world literally requires, and has, a creator, and that the story's real question is which of its two central characters actually holds that role.

distinctive_terms.label: Descartes
distinctive_terms.note: An explicit philosophical anchor for Allison's solipsism, marking the story's premise as a deliberate engagement with Cartesian doubt about the reality of other minds.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: No commentary by Dick on this specific story was found in this evidence pass.

open_questions: Is there documented commentary from Dick on his choice to stage solipsism literally rather than as psychological metaphor, and on the story's explicit Descartes/Plato references?
Is this story ever discussed alongside Dick's later, more developed treatments of private or competing realities (e.g., Eye in the Sky, Ubik) as an early, compact prototype?
Is Larry's own unconscious possession of reality-shaping power -- discovered only in the act of using it -- ever read by critics as a comment on how such power operates invisibly until challenged?
